transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. I'm Dr. [Your Name]. What brings you in today?

Hi, Doctor. I... well, I know I need to be here because I just can't stop worrying about everything. And I mean literally everything at once. It's like my brain has a dozen browser tabs open and they're all playing different audio at the same time, you know? I work in tech, so maybe that's just the analogy I jump to, but... I'm constantly terrified I'm slipping at work. Like, I'll stare at a project and suddenly I'm convinced I'm messing everything up and I'm going to get fired. 

And if I get fired, how do we pay the bills? The bills are always on my mind anyway. Even though we're technically doing okay right now, I just obsess over every single expense. And then that bleeds into my marriage. I just keep thinking I'm failing my wife, and failing as a father. I can't even finish simple things around the house anymore. There are all these house projects I started, like fixing the drywall in the hallway and sorting out the garage, and I just keep dropping them halfway through because I get so overwhelmed by everything else. So now there's just half-finished stuff everywhere, which just makes me feel even worse, like I'm basically just a complete failure as a husband and a dad. It's just this endless cycle of worrying about my job, the house, my family, the money... all of it, all at once, all the time, and I just can't shut it off.
Do you find that your anxiety is present most days and seems to jump from one concern to another, even when things are going relatively well?

Yeah, it's... it's literally every single day. And you hit the nail on the head about it jumping around, especially when things are actually fine. Like, we could have plenty of money in the checking account, the kids are healthy, work is fine, but it doesn't matter. I'll sit down at my desk, right? And I'll explicitly tell myself to just focus on the code in front of me. Just look at the screen, write the function, do your job. Or, you know, even if I'm trying to burn off the stress, if I'm at the gym, I'll tell myself, just breathe through this workout, just focus on your form and get through the set. 

But it's impossible. I just can't control it. It's like... it's like one concern just physically hooks into another one, like a chain pulling me under. I'll be looking at that code, and then I'll think about a potential bug, and before I can even stop myself, I'm twenty steps ahead in this massive worst-case scenario. I'm sitting there vividly imagining this tiny mistake turning into a terrible performance review, which turns into me losing my job, and then suddenly we can't pay the mortgage and my family is just so much worse off, all because of me. And I'm just standing there on the treadmill or staring at my monitor, completely paralyzed by this future that hasn't even happened. I just can't stop the chain reaction once it starts. It just goes and goes and goes, and I can't break out of it no matter how hard I try to just rein my thoughts in.
Do you experience any physical symptoms like restlessness, fatigue, trouble concentrating, muscle tension, or sleep disturbances because of all this worrying?

Yeah, physically, it's... it's a lot. I feel wound up so tight, pretty much all day long. Like, my shoulders, for instance... they are just completely locked up. I actually bought this incredibly expensive ergonomic chair for my desk a few months ago, thinking maybe it was just my posture from coding, you know? Because I'm at the computer for like eight, ten hours a day and I thought, okay, it's just bad posture. But it's not the chair at all. It's me. I'm just constantly bracing myself, like physically tensing my whole upper body, waiting for some kind of impact or bad news that never actually comes. I'll catch myself with my shoulders practically shrugged up to my ears, and I have to consciously force them down, but literally five minutes later, they're right back up there again. 

And the restlessness... well, sitting still has become basically impossible for me. If I have a gap between Zoom meetings—or honestly, even during them if I can get away with turning my camera off—I can't just sit in my chair. I end up pacing. I'll pace back and forth across my home office, just wearing a track in the rug, trying to burn off this... this nervous energy, I guess. I'll walk into the hallway, look at that drywall project I mentioned earlier, get stressed about it, walk back to the desk, just back and forth, back and forth. 

It's even bleeding into my hobbies, which is incredibly frustrating. I go to this local chess club on Thursday nights. I've been going for a couple of years since grad school, and it used to be my way to unwind, to just use my brain in a structured, quiet way, right? But lately, I can't even sit quietly at the board. I catch myself constantly tapping the captured pieces on the table, just tap-tap-tapping, or bouncing my leg so hard the table vibrates. The other guys have started giving me looks, and I feel terrible about it, but I just... I physically cannot just sit and exist. It's like there's a motor inside me that's just stuck on overdrive.
Can you think of a time in the past six months when you were not feeling anxious or worried about something for at least a few consecutive days?

Six months? God, no. No, not even close. Honestly, if I trace it all back, this has been going on for about nine months now. It hasn't stopped once. I know exactly when it really locked in, too, because it was right around the time the cloud migration at work really ramped up. 

We were transitioning all our legacy servers—stuff that had basically been duct-taped together since before I even got my master's—and the sheer volume of things that could go wrong was just staggering. I was practically living at my desk, terrified I'd push one wrong configuration and wipe out terabytes of client data or crash the whole platform. And, you know, because I was constantly on edge from that... well, that's exactly when the arguments at home started becoming a regular thing. 

My wife would just ask me a simple question, like about when I was going to finish that drywall in the hallway, and I would just completely overload. It turned into this awful routine where I was stressed about the migration, which made me totally unavailable mentally, which led to us fighting, which just added to the massive pile of things I felt like I was failing at. The arguments just became part of the daily schedule. So, yeah, it’s been nine solid months of this. I genuinely cannot remember a single day in that entire window—let alone a few consecutive days—where my brain just let me be. Even on a Saturday, even if the servers are fine and nobody is arguing, I'm just sitting there waiting for the other shoe to drop. It’s just been this relentless hum every single minute since that migration started.
Do you feel that your anxiety and worrying are out of your control, even when you consciously try to stop them?

Yeah, it's... I mean, I think I touched on this a bit earlier, but it is completely out of my hands. I try, doctor, I really do try to just shut it down. Like I said, I'll be sitting there, staring at my monitor, and I will literally have this internal monologue where I'm saying, "Okay, just look at the IDE. Just look at the code. You have one function to write. Just focus on the syntax, write the tests, commit the code." Or, you know, I'll be at the gym, which is supposed to be my outlet, right? And I'm telling myself, "Just breathe. In through the nose, out through the mouth. Just focus on the rep. Just get through the set." 

But it just... it doesn't matter what I tell myself. It’s like trying to stop a freight train with a piece of paper. The thoughts just completely hijack my brain. One concern just hooks right into the next one, and it's instantaneous. It's not like a slow build where I can catch it. I'll look at a line of code, worry about a potential edge case bug, and then boom, my brain is off to the races. I'm suddenly twenty steps ahead. I'm not even in the room anymore. I'm sitting there vividly picturing this bug getting past QA, going into production, crashing a client's system. And then I'm in my boss's office getting this horrific performance review, and then I'm packing up my desk because I've been fired. And then, you know, the real panic sets in because I'm thinking about the mortgage, and how we're going to pay for groceries, and how my wife is going to react, and how my kids are going to suffer because I couldn't write a simple piece of code properly. 

It just spirals so fast, and I'm just trapped in it. I can feel my heart racing, I can feel the panic, and I'm consciously telling myself, "This hasn't happened. Stop it. You're just writing code." But the rational part of my brain has zero control over it. It just runs and runs until it exhausts me, and there is absolutely nothing I can do to hit the brakes.
Have there been times when you've felt so overwhelmed by your anxiety that you've avoided certain situations, tasks, or even people because you knew it would make your worrying worse?

Avoided? No... no, I don't think so. I mean, honestly, I wish I had the luxury of just avoiding things, but I don't. It's actually kind of the opposite, if that makes sense? I just white-knuckle my way through absolutely everything. 

Like, take those Zoom meetings I mentioned earlier. I know going into our weekly architecture review that my heart is going to be pounding out of my chest. I know I'm going to be sweating through my shirt, terrified that the lead engineer is going to poke a hole in my deployment strategy or find some flaw in the server logic. I know it's going to be a solid hour of pure, concentrated misery where I'm just waiting to be exposed as a fraud. But I still log on. I'm always there at 9:58 AM for a 10:00 AM call, sitting in that stupid expensive chair, just dreading it, but I never skip it. I don't call in sick. I don't make up excuses. 

And it's the same with people and stuff around the house. I don't avoid my wife, even though I know there's a really high chance she might ask about the hallway drywall or the kids' schedules, which I know is going to instantly add to that massive mental pile and probably trigger another argument. I still sit down at the dinner table every single night. I'm physically there, eating whatever she cooked, even if my brain is completely fried and I'm practically vibrating out of my skin with worry. 

Or the chess club—I told you how bad that's gotten, right? With the leg bouncing and the tapping. It's humiliating. I know exactly how it's going to go before I even get in the car to drive over to the community center on Thursday nights. I know I'm going to be a nervous wreck, I know I won't be able to focus on the openings, and I know I'm going to annoy the other guys at the tables next to me. But I still drive there. I still walk in, I still shake hands, I still set up the board. I don't hide from any of it. I just... I just endure it. It's like I have this ingrained compulsion that I have to keep functioning, I have to keep doing the tasks and seeing the people, even though every single alarm bell in my head is screaming at me to just run away and hide under the covers. So, no, I haven't been avoiding anything at all. I just suffer through it in plain sight.

Do you find that your anxiety and worry often shifts between different areas of your life, such as work, relationships, health, and daily responsibilities, rather than focusing on just one specific thing?

Shifts? Yeah, but it's almost like it doesn't even have the decency to just be one thing at a time. It's more like... well, honestly, that's exactly why I finally made the appointment to come see you in the first place. I came in because I just can't stop worrying about absolutely everything at once. It’s like having fifty browser tabs open in my head and they’re all playing different audio at max volume, and I can't figure out which one is making the noise, so I just hear all of it, all the time. 

I'll be sitting there worrying about whether I'm slipping at work—you know, with the migration and the server logic, terrified I'm missing something critical that's going to get me fired. But then, almost in the exact same breath, the focus just violently swings over to my marriage, and I'm obsessing over the tension with my wife and analyzing every single word of our last argument. And then, boom, it's the bills. I'm suddenly doing mental math on our mortgage and the utilities, thinking about how expensive groceries have gotten and what happens if my salary disappears. 

And then, before I can even process the financial panic, I'm thinking about the house. Like that stupid unfinished drywall in the hallway I mentioned, or the gutters that need cleaning—all these house projects I just keep dropping or putting off because I'm too mentally exhausted to even hold a hammer when I log off for the day. It just bounces from work, to money, to the house, to my marriage... and it all just culminates in this massive, crushing feeling that I am basically failing as a husband and a father. I mean, how can I be a good dad or a supportive partner when my brain is constantly looping through this endless checklist of impending disasters? It never just stays on the code, or just on the house. It bleeds into every single corner of my life. So, yeah, it definitely shifts, but it's more like a constant, exhausting rotation where everything feels like a priority-one emergency, and I never get a break from any of it.
Has your excessive anxiety and worry occurred on more days than not for at least six months?

Oh, easily. More days than not? Try every single day. I mean, six months... yeah, it’s definitely been longer than that. If I really sit down and trace it back, this has been going on for about nine months now. A solid nine months of just... relentless, non-stop worrying. 

I can actually pinpoint exactly when it started getting this bad, because it was right when the big cloud migration project at work really ramped up. We were transitioning all our legacy databases, and the sheer volume of things that could go catastrophically wrong just exploded overnight. I was suddenly the point guy for ensuring the data integrity during the transfer, and the pressure was just... I mean, it was suffocating. I'd be sitting there staring at the architecture diagrams, realizing that if one script failed, we'd corrupt client data, and I just couldn't shake the dread. 

And then, because I was constantly on edge about the migration and working myself into the ground, my fuse at home was just completely shot. That’s exactly when the arguments with my wife started becoming a regular thing. Like, really regular, almost daily. She’d ask me a simple question about, I don't know, picking up the kids from practice or fixing that hallway drywall I keep bringing up, and I’d just snap. Or I'd completely zone out because my brain was still stuck on server configurations, and she'd get upset that I wasn't listening. And then we'd fight about me not being present, which just added this massive layer of guilt and panic about my marriage failing right on top of my career tanking. 

So it was this perfect storm. The migration ramped up, the fights at home became our new normal, and all of that was about nine months ago. And since then, I honestly don't think I've had a single day where my brain has actually turned off or given me a break. So, yes, to answer your question, it definitely clears the six-month mark by a long shot.
Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in activities you used to enjoy during this time?

Down? Hopeless? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. It’s really not a sadness thing, if that makes sense. I’m not sitting around crying or feeling like life is pointless. Honestly, in a weird way, I almost wish I could just stop caring. If I had actually lost interest in things, maybe I wouldn't be so stressed out about all of it! But I still care. I care way too much, about absolutely everything. 

And as for losing interest in activities... no, the interest is definitely still there. Like, take the chess club I was telling you about. I still love chess. I really do. I still buy the strategy books, I still lie awake in bed at 2:00 AM watching grandmaster matches on YouTube on my phone when I should be sleeping. The desire to do the things I used to enjoy hasn't gone away at all. It's just that when I actually try to do them—when I physically sit down at the board—my brain is so completely hijacked by the server migration, or the mortgage, or the drywall, that I just can't be present to actually enjoy it. But the interest itself? It's 100% still there. I want to enjoy it so badly. 

And it's the same with feeling hopeless. I don't feel hopeless. I'm actually desperately trying to fix everything all the time. I'm constantly trying to problem-solve, running through all these worst-case scenarios so I can prevent them from happening. If I were hopeless, I feel like I would just give up, right? I'd just let the servers crash at work. I'd let my wife get mad and I wouldn't even try to explain myself or fix the tension. But I'm fighting it every single second of every single day. I'm trying so hard to keep all the plates spinning. So, no, I definitely don't feel down or depressed or anything like that. I'm just... I'm just so wired and tense. It's not that I've given up on life, it's just that I'm constantly terrified everything in my life is about to fall apart.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of avoidance related to the anxiety, which would support a diagnosis of GAD (F41.1) over adjustment disorder with anxiety (F43.22).
doctor.question: Have there been times when you've felt so overwhelmed by your anxiety that you've avoided certain situations, tasks, or even people because you knew it would make your worrying worse?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about avoidance behaviors (avoiding situations, tasks, or people), which is not listed in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Avoided? No... no, I don't think so. I mean, honestly, I wish I had the luxury of just avoiding things, but I don't. It's actually kind of the opposite, if that makes sense? I just white-knuckle my way through absolutely everything. 

Like, take those Zoom meetings I mentioned earlier. I know going into our weekly architecture review that my heart is going to be pounding out of my chest. I know I'm going to be sweating through my shirt, terrified that the lead engineer is going to poke a hole in my deployment strategy or find some flaw in the server logic. I know it's going to be a solid hour of pure, concentrated misery where I'm just waiting to be exposed as a fraud. But I still log on. I'm always there at 9:58 AM for a 10:00 AM call, sitting in that stupid expensive chair, just dreading it, but I never skip it. I don't call in sick. I don't make up excuses. 

And it's the same with people and stuff around the house. I don't avoid my wife, even though I know there's a really high chance she might ask about the hallway drywall or the kids' schedules, which I know is going to instantly add to that massive mental pile and probably trigger another argument. I still sit down at the dinner table every single night. I'm physically there, eating whatever she cooked, even if my brain is completely fried and I'm practically vibrating out of my skin with worry. 

Or the chess club—I told you how bad that's gotten, right? With the leg bouncing and the tapping. It's humiliating. I know exactly how it's going to go before I even get in the car to drive over to the community center on Thursday nights. I know I'm going to be a nervous wreck, I know I won't be able to focus on the openings, and I know I'm going to annoy the other guys at the tables next to me. But I still drive there. I still walk in, I still shake hands, I still set up the board. I don't hide from any of it. I just... I just endure it. It's like I have this ingrained compulsion that I have to keep functioning, I have to keep doing the tasks and seeing the people, even though every single alarm bell in my head is screaming at me to just run away and hide under the covers. So, no, I haven't been avoiding anything at all. I just suffer through it in plain sight.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive anxiety and worry about a number of events or activities (i.e., not limited to one specific area), which is a key differentiator for Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) over Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22).
doctor.question: Do you find that your anxiety and worry often shifts between different areas of your life, such as work, relationships, health, and daily responsibilities, rather than focusing on just one specific thing?

target_item.name: Excessive_Anxiety_Worry
target_item.manifestation: I came in because I can't stop worrying about everything at once—my marriage, whether I'm slipping at work, bills, the house projects I keep dropping, and whether I'm basically failing as a husband and father.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the anxiety involves multiple different areas of life (work, relationships, responsibilities), which directly maps to excessive worry about a number of events or activities.

patient.answer:
Shifts? Yeah, but it's almost like it doesn't even have the decency to just be one thing at a time. It's more like... well, honestly, that's exactly why I finally made the appointment to come see you in the first place. I came in because I just can't stop worrying about absolutely everything at once. It’s like having fifty browser tabs open in my head and they’re all playing different audio at max volume, and I can't figure out which one is making the noise, so I just hear all of it, all the time. 

I'll be sitting there worrying about whether I'm slipping at work—you know, with the migration and the server logic, terrified I'm missing something critical that's going to get me fired. But then, almost in the exact same breath, the focus just violently swings over to my marriage, and I'm obsessing over the tension with my wife and analyzing every single word of our last argument. And then, boom, it's the bills. I'm suddenly doing mental math on our mortgage and the utilities, thinking about how expensive groceries have gotten and what happens if my salary disappears. 

And then, before I can even process the financial panic, I'm thinking about the house. Like that stupid unfinished drywall in the hallway I mentioned, or the gutters that need cleaning—all these house projects I just keep dropping or putting off because I'm too mentally exhausted to even hold a hammer when I log off for the day. It just bounces from work, to money, to the house, to my marriage... and it all just culminates in this massive, crushing feeling that I am basically failing as a husband and a father. I mean, how can I be a good dad or a supportive partner when my brain is constantly looping through this endless checklist of impending disasters? It never just stays on the code, or just on the house. It bleeds into every single corner of my life. So, yeah, it definitely shifts, but it's more like a constant, exhausting rotation where everything feels like a priority-one emergency, and I never get a break from any of it.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences excessive anxiety and worry more days than not for at least six months, which is a key criterion for GAD.
doctor.question: Has your excessive anxiety and worry occurred on more days than not for at least six months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about nine months, since the cloud migration ramped up and the arguments at home started becoming a regular thing.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the anxiety and worry have been present for at least six months, which directly relates to the duration of my symptoms.

patient.answer:
Oh, easily. More days than not? Try every single day. I mean, six months... yeah, it’s definitely been longer than that. If I really sit down and trace it back, this has been going on for about nine months now. A solid nine months of just... relentless, non-stop worrying. 

I can actually pinpoint exactly when it started getting this bad, because it was right when the big cloud migration project at work really ramped up. We were transitioning all our legacy databases, and the sheer volume of things that could go catastrophically wrong just exploded overnight. I was suddenly the point guy for ensuring the data integrity during the transfer, and the pressure was just... I mean, it was suffocating. I'd be sitting there staring at the architecture diagrams, realizing that if one script failed, we'd corrupt client data, and I just couldn't shake the dread. 

And then, because I was constantly on edge about the migration and working myself into the ground, my fuse at home was just completely shot. That’s exactly when the arguments with my wife started becoming a regular thing. Like, really regular, almost daily. She’d ask me a simple question about, I don't know, picking up the kids from practice or fixing that hallway drywall I keep bringing up, and I’d just snap. Or I'd completely zone out because my brain was still stuck on server configurations, and she'd get upset that I wasn't listening. And then we'd fight about me not being present, which just added this massive layer of guilt and panic about my marriage failing right on top of my career tanking. 

So it was this perfect storm. The migration ramped up, the fights at home became our new normal, and all of that was about nine months ago. And since then, I honestly don't think I've had a single day where my brain has actually turned off or given me a break. So, yes, to answer your question, it definitely clears the six-month mark by a long shot.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences symptoms of depression, which would support a diagnosis of Generalized Anxiety Disorder (F41.1) over Adjustment Disorder with Anxiety (F43.22), as GAD often includes comorbid depressive features.
doctor.question: Have you noticed yourself feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest in activities you used to enjoy during this time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of depression (feeling down, hopeless, or losing interest), which are not covered by the Generalized Anxiety Disorder symptom profile provided.

patient.answer:
Down? Hopeless? No... no, I wouldn't say that at all. It’s really not a sadness thing, if that makes sense. I’m not sitting around crying or feeling like life is pointless. Honestly, in a weird way, I almost wish I could just stop caring. If I had actually lost interest in things, maybe I wouldn't be so stressed out about all of it! But I still care. I care way too much, about absolutely everything. 

And as for losing interest in activities... no, the interest is definitely still there. Like, take the chess club I was telling you about. I still love chess. I really do. I still buy the strategy books, I still lie awake in bed at 2:00 AM watching grandmaster matches on YouTube on my phone when I should be sleeping. The desire to do the things I used to enjoy hasn't gone away at all. It's just that when I actually try to do them—when I physically sit down at the board—my brain is so completely hijacked by the server migration, or the mortgage, or the drywall, that I just can't be present to actually enjoy it. But the interest itself? It's 100% still there. I want to enjoy it so badly. 

And it's the same with feeling hopeless. I don't feel hopeless. I'm actually desperately trying to fix everything all the time. I'm constantly trying to problem-solve, running through all these worst-case scenarios so I can prevent them from happening. If I were hopeless, I feel like I would just give up, right? I'd just let the servers crash at work. I'd let my wife get mad and I wouldn't even try to explain myself or fix the tension. But I'm fighting it every single second of every single day. I'm trying so hard to keep all the plates spinning. So, no, I definitely don't feel down or depressed or anything like that. I'm just... I'm just so wired and tense. It's not that I've given up on life, it's just that I'm constantly terrified everything in my life is about to fall apart.
